newsletter.subject: Fall Fest fills Baker Creek, Latin.Knox takes Printshop on First Friday, and goats on the Kern's lawn

feature.label: Urban Wilderness
feature.title: AMBC's Fall Fest fills Baker Creek with group rides, a Whip Off, five bands and a lit-up jump line Friday and Saturday
feature.deck: Free, and the trails are the point.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Fri Nov 6 · 5 – 10 PM · Sat Nov 7 · 8:30 AM – midnight

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Baker Creek Preserve and Urban Wilderness Gateway Park · 1516 Taylor Rd

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: Free · beer garden and food trucks on site · the bike raffle and silent auction are the fundraiser

facts.label: Friday
facts.value: Knoxville Utility Band 5:30 · pump track and jump line lit at 6:30 · Best Day Ever film 6:45 · Adventure Slideshows 8 · after-party at Climbing Roots 10

facts.label: Saturday rides
facts.value: Joy Ride and adaptive-bike demos 9:30 · social, advanced and vintage rides 10 · South Loop ride noon · bike parade 12:30 · kids' rides 1 · Whip Off at Devil's Racetrack 3 · strider race 4:45

facts.label: Saturday stage
facts.value: Mal Nombre noon · Mercy Lights 5 · Butcherbird 6 · Best Line Invitational 7 · Megaweed 8:15 · raffle drawing 9 · New Speedway Honkers 9:30 · silent disco 10:30

facts.label: Parking

facts.label: Weather
facts.value: Friday partly sunny and 70, 45 overnight · Saturday mostly sunny and 66

body.text: The Appalachian Mountain Bike Club calls Fall Fest its homecoming, and the 17th one lands this weekend at Baker Creek Preserve, the gateway to the Urban Wilderness at the end of James White Parkway. It is the club's biggest fundraiser of the year and it costs nothing to walk in: two days of guided rides for every speed, kids' events, a jump contest, a night-time jump exhibition, five bands on a main stage and a beer garden, with a bike raffle and a silent auction paying for the trails. Riders come from around the country for it. Most of the people on the lawn are from around here.
Friday night

Friday is the easy half. The campground and beer garden open at five, the Knoxville Utility Band plays bluegrass on the main stage at 5:30, and at 6:30 the pump track and the jump line are lit for Friday Night Lights, which is exactly what it sounds like. At 6:45 Catalyst Sports shows the film Best Day Ever, and at eight nine women tell their biggest adventures in the PechaKucha format, twenty slides at twenty seconds each, under the stars. Last call is 9:30 and the after-party moves to Climbing Roots, the bouldering gym. A quarter of Friday's beer profits go to Catalyst Sports, which runs adaptive mountain biking.
Saturday

Saturday starts with coffee at 8:30 and rides at 9:30: the women's Joy Ride, adaptive-bike demos, then at ten a social ride, an advanced long ride with Tennessee Valley Bikes, a vintage mountain bike ride with Two Bikes and a shuttle to Devil's Racetrack. At noon Mal Nombre plays and Harper's leads the South Loop ride. The bike parade at 12:30 is for everyone, decorated or not; at one the kids ride with Trail Blazers and the jump line is women-only for an hour. The Whip Off at three is the crowd event: riders send the big jumps at the bottom of Devil's Racetrack and anyone can enter until 2:30 at the booth, men, women and groms. The strider race for the smallest riders is at 4:45.

After dark the main stage takes over: Mercy Lights at five, Butcherbird at six, and at seven the Best Line Invitational puts invited pro and local riders on the lit jump line with commentary and cash prizes. Megaweed plays at 8:15, the silent auction closes at 8:30, the bike raffle is drawn at nine, New Speedway Honkers close the stage at 9:30 and a silent disco runs until the festival turns in at midnight.
The practical part

Parking is free at the Baker Creek Bottoms overflow lot, at South Doyle Middle School after five on Friday, and at the Gateway Park lot under Sevierville Pike; the club asks everyone to stay off the neighborhood streets. Camping on the site is free and first come, with portable toilets and nothing else, no fires. Friday is partly sunny and 70 before dropping to 45 overnight, and Saturday is mostly sunny and 66, so the night events want a jacket.

stories.deck: Starts with the classics, goes underground.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Fri Nov 6 · 9 PM till close

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Printshop Beer Co. · 1532 Island Home Ave

facts.label: The DJs

body.text: Latin.Knox, the Latin house party that debuted in July, comes to Printshop for its second night on First Friday. The promoter's pitch is a set that starts familiar and gets deeper as the night goes: DJ EV opens with the Latin party classics and club bangers he plays around Knoxville, Jason Davila, out of Atlanta's underground dance parties, takes the peak, and Minitiger, the Knoxville fixture who closed Fly by Night's Halloween ball, finishes with Latin-infused selections. Nine o'clock, twenty dollars, twenty-one and up, in the taproom on the river at 1532 Island Home Avenue. Knox Social Girls Club is folding its Latin Ladies Night into the same party, and says you do not have to be Latina to come. Printshop's Friday flight deal, twelve dollars for four pours, runs from noon to nine if you want to get there early.

body.text: The 808, the music venue that opened at 808 Sevier Avenue in October with national touring acts, gives Friday to the locals. College Night is three Knoxville bands on the hour, Ella Pinchock at eight, Fort Knox at nine and Pocket Ace at ten, with the doors at seven. It is five dollars at the door and free for anyone who RSVPs on the venue's Posh page, eighteen and up. The room's own line is come out and support the city's local talent. stories.title: SoKno Sourdough's First Friday pairs artist Peter Riesing with Paradise Chocolate's new chocolate tonic
stories.deck: A bakery, a painter and a drink to taste.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Fri Nov 6 · First Friday evening

facts.label: Where
facts.value: SoKno Sourdough · 2006 Barber St, between Redbud Kitchen and Hi-Wire

facts.label: On
facts.value: Work by Peter Riesing · Paradise Chocolate bars · samples of a chocolate tonic

body.text: SoKno Sourdough, the all-sourdough bakery on Barber Street, opens its doors for First Friday with Peter Riesing's art on the walls and Paradise Chocolate at a table. Paradise, the Knoxville bean-to-bar maker, was at the bakery for an earlier First Friday and is back with its bars and something new from its kitchen: a chocolate tonic, which it will be pouring as samples. The bakery and the chocolate are both small, woman-run South Knoxville businesses, and this is the kind of evening where you meet the people who make the thing. Paradise moves on to the Drop Inn's fire pit for Fall Fest on Saturday with s'mores and drinking chocolate.

body.text: Cut Corners, the Atlanta collective that describes itself as engineering random acts of creativity through music, dancing and interactive art, is on tour and taking over Fly by Night, the seventies cocktail lounge on Sevier Avenue, on Saturday. Their own announcement promises a toolbox of bouncy techno, banging club and bubbling house from nine until one, ten dollars at the door. Fly by Night is the lounge that ran four Halloween nights in a row last week, so the floor is warmed up. Kentucky kicks off against the Vols at 6:15 Saturday; the game should be done around the time the first DJ goes on, and the Sevier Avenue bars will be emptying out of the fourth quarter.

body.text: Knox Vintage Pet Project is the small rescue that finds homes for the old dogs and the ones with medical bills, and Bow Wow Bingo is how it pays for them. Sunday's is at Printshop from two to four: bingo cards, cold beer, and foster dogs walking the patio looking for a lap. The rescue's own rule is that it is kid friendly, dog friendly and beer friendly, so bring the leash and the stroller. Last month's bingo was at Alliance Brewing; this one moves up Island Home Avenue to the brewery on the river, and the forecast is mostly sunny and 65, a patio day.

stories.title: Moss Meander walks Mead's Quarry with a naturalist and a hand lens Saturday afternoon
stories.deck: Moss holds the story of the forest.

facts.label: When

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $15, plus the site's ticket fee

facts.label: Before you go

body.text: Moss, the park says, is where children learned to look for fairies, and it is also an organism that holds the story of the forest in its structure. Moss Meander is two hours at Mead's Quarry with an Ijams Nature Center naturalist, learning to tell the species apart and what each one says about the ground it grows on, at the one time of year the moss is the greenest thing in the woods. Meet at the picnic tables by the quarry lot at two; it is fifteen dollars, for ages sixteen and up, and the walk is on uneven trail. Saturday is mostly sunny and 66.

stories.title: Wilderness Basics teaches shelter, fire and food in three hours at Ijams Nature Center Saturday
stories.deck: Thrive, not just survive, the park says.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Sat Nov 7 · 9 AM – noon

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Ijams Nature Center · 2915 Island Home Ave

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $15, plus the site's ticket fee · parking free for participants

facts.label: Terrain
facts.value: Up to a mile over rocks, roots and gravel

body.text: Outside can be a scary place, the course description admits: bears, winter storms, critters and mountains. Wilderness Basics is the park's introductory answer, three hours on Saturday morning learning to prioritize in a survival scenario, build a shelter, start and keep a fire, and find and store food, with some walking between the lessons. It is for ages fourteen and up, fifteen dollars, and it starts at nine from the visitor center at 2915 Island Home Avenue with the parking fee waived for the class. The waiver at ijams.org/waiver covers you for the year.

stories.label: Ijams Nature Center
stories.title: Bird banding at Meads Quarry puts songbirds in gloved hands for five dollars Sunday morning
stories.deck: Behind the scenes at the banding station.

facts.label: When
facts.value: Sun Nov 8 · 8 – 9:30 AM

facts.label: Where
facts.value: Meads Quarry lot · 3526 Island Home Ave · a staff member walks the group five minutes to the station

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $5, plus the site's ticket fee · no parking fee for the program

facts.label: Before you go
facts.value: Sign the park's yearly waiver at ijams.org/waiver

body.text: The Ijams community science team runs a bird banding station in the woods behind Meads Quarry, and a few mornings a season it lets the public in. Sunday's is one: at eight the group meets in the quarry lot, walks five minutes to the station and watches migratory and resident songbirds safely netted, measured, banded and released, the data going toward the health of the birds around South Knoxville. Five dollars is the whole ticket, it is ninety minutes, and November is late migration, so the nets catch the birds that stay. It is 41 at dawn Sunday and clear.

stories.label: Old Sevier
stories.title: City Council overturns the Kerbela apartments, 5-4, and the old Shriners site goes back to square one
stories.deck: We told you approved in August. Not anymore.

facts.label: Decided
facts.value: Tue Oct 13 · Knoxville City Council, 5-4

facts.label: Site
facts.value: 315 Kerbela Ave · 5.7 acres at Sevier Ave & Dawson St

facts.label: The plan
facts.value: 225 apartments · 55-and-over community · CR Endeavors

facts.label: Next
facts.value: A new proposal, a lawsuit or dropping it · the developer hasn't said

body.text: In August we reported that the Planning Commission had approved 225 apartments for people 55 and over on the old Kerbela Shriners site, and that design and permitting came next. They don't, for now. On October 13 City Council upheld an appeal from members of the South Waterfront Advisory and Advocacy Group and overturned that approval, 5-4. The commission's own vote had been 7-6.

The fight was over seven exceptions the developer, CR Endeavors, wanted from the South Waterfront code. The company says the site's unusual terrain makes it hard to meet every requirement. Council attorney Rob Frost said the vote turned on whether the project met the code's intent, and that this was the first appeal of its kind ever to reach the council. Debbie Helsley, Lynne Fugate, Denzel Grant and Doug Lloyd voted for the apartments.

CR Endeavors can bring a new proposal, walk away, or take it to Knox County Chancery Court, and Frost said it has 60 days to file suit. The company said in October that it would evaluate its next steps, and we found no announcement as of Monday. The Shriners still owned the land as of the last reports. We'll be watching.
